etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English ernest, eornest, from Old English eornest, eornost, eornust (“earnestness, zeal, seriousness, battle”), from Proto-Germanic *ernustuz (“earnest, strength, solidity, struggle, fight”), a derivative of Proto-Germanic *arniz (“efficient, capable, diligent, sure”), from Proto-Indo-European *er- (“to cause to move, arouse, increase”).

Cognate with West Frisian earnst (“earnest, seriousness”), Dutch ernst (“seriousness, gravity, earnest”), German Ernst (“seriousness, earnestness, zeal, vigour”), Icelandic ern (“brisk, vigorous”), Gothic 𐌰𐍂𐌽𐌹𐌱𐌰 (arniba, “secure, certain, sure”).

The adjective is from Middle English eornest, from Old English eornoste (“earnest, zealous, serious”), from the noun. Cognate with North Frisian ernste (“earnest”), Middle Low German ernest, ernst (“serious, earnest”), German ernst (“serious, earnest”).

quote.citation: a. 1587, Philippe Sidnei [i.e., Philip Sidney], “(please specify the folio)”, in [Fulke Greville; Matthew Gwinne; John Florio], editors, The Countesse of Pembrokes Arcadia [The New Arcadia], London:  […]  [John Windet] for William Ponsonbie, published 1590, →OCLC:
quote.text: Take heed that this jest do not one day turn to earnest.

quote.citation: c. 1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Richard the Third: […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: That high All-Seer which I dallied with / Hath turn'd my feigned prayer on my head / And given in earnest what I begg'd in jest.

quote.citation: 1914, February 13, The Times, Obituary: Canon Augustus Jessopp
quote.text: He wrote well in a forcible, colloquial style, with the air of being tremendously in earnest, and full of knowledge which overflowed his pages, tricked out with somewhat boisterous illustrations.

definitions.definition: Seriousness; reality; actuality (as opposed to joking or pretence)
(transitive) To be serious with; use in earnest.

quote.citation: 1602, Pastor Fido, (Please provide the book title or journal name):
quote.text: Let's prove among ourselves our armes in jest, That when we come to earnest them with men, We may them better use.

definitions.definition: (said of an action or an utterance) Serious, sincere, ingenuous.
(with a positive sense) Focused in the pursuit of an objective; honestly eager to obtain or do.
Intent; focused; showing a lot of concentration.
(said of a person or a person's character) Possessing or characterised by seriousness.
Serious; weighty; of a serious, weighty, or important nature; important.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Uncertain; apparently related to erres. Compare also arles.

definitions.definition: A sum of money paid in advance as a deposit; hence, a pledge, a guarantee, an indication of something to come.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 2 Corinthians 5:5:
quote.text: Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit.

quote.citation: 1624, John Donne, “19. Prayer”, in Deuotions upon Emergent Occasions, and Seuerall Steps in My Sicknes: […], London:  […]  A[ugustine] M[atthews] for Thomas Iones, →OCLC, page 508:
quote.text: As therefore the morning devv, is a pavvne of the evenings fatneſſe, ſo, O Lord, let this daies comfort be the earneſt of to morrowes,  […]

quote.citation: 1837, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], Ethel Churchill: Or, The Two Brides. […], volume II, London: Henry Colburn, […], →OCLC, pages 152–153:
quote.text: The vanity is at once encouraged and gratified; while the present small triumph is too readily taken as earnest for a greater one.

quote.citation: 1990, Peter Hopkirk, The Great Game, Folio Society, published 2010, page 365:
quote.text: But if all this was viewed by Gladstone and the Cabinet as an earnest of St Petersburg's future good intentions in Central Asia, then disillusionment was soon to follow.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From earn +‎ -est.
